items.q: Define society, government and caste.
items.a: Society: an organised group of people living together with shared customs and institutions. Government: the machinery through which the will of the state is formulated and carried out. Caste: a hereditary, birth-based social group, arranged in a hierarchy, that traditionally fixed a person's occupation and status.

items.q: Define a casteless society.
items.a: A casteless society is one where people are not divided or ranked by caste at birth, and everyone is treated as equal in dignity, rights and opportunities.

items.q: What do you mean by caste discrimination?
items.a: Caste discrimination is unequal and unfair treatment of people because of the caste they are born into, such as untouchability, denial of temple entry, education, land or jobs, and social exclusion.

items.q: What is equality?
items.a: Equality means all people have equal worth and are given equal rights and equal opportunities without discrimination of caste, religion, gender, race or wealth; it is essential for social justice.

items.q: What is exploitation?
items.a: Exploitation is the unfair use of people or resources for one's own benefit, e.g., making people work without fair wages, bonded labour or child labour. The Constitution prohibits it under Articles 23 and 24.

items.q: Define caste violence.
items.a: Caste violence is violence committed against people because of their caste, usually by dominant castes against the oppressed, such as attacks, killings, honour crimes and destruction of property.

items.q: Explain the temple entry movement.
items.a: Temple entry movements fought for the right of the so-called untouchable castes to enter Hindu temples. Examples: the Vaikom Satyagraha (1924-25) led by Periyar and others, the Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931-32), and Vaidyanatha Iyer's entry into the Madurai Meenakshi temple (1939). Laws such as the Madras Temple Entry Authorisation Act (1939, 1947) followed.

items.q: Write a note on the reservation policy.
items.a: Reservation reserves a share of seats in education, jobs and legislatures for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs, to redress historic injustice. Articles 15(4) and 16(4) (First Amendment, 1951) allow it. Tamil Nadu has 69% reservation (BC 30%, MBC 20%, SC 18%, ST 1%), protected in the Ninth Schedule by the 76th Amendment. At the centre, OBCs get 27% (Mandal), and the Supreme Court has fixed a 50% ceiling in general.

items.q: Write about equality in the Indian Constitution.
items.a: The Preamble promises equality of status and opportunity. Articles 14-18 guarantee equality before law, no discrimination, equal opportunity in public employment, abolition of untouchability and titles. Articles 15(4) and 16(4) allow special provisions for backward classes. Article 39 (DPSP) seeks equal pay for equal work.

items.q: Give a brief account of caste organisations.
items.a: Caste organisations are associations formed by members of a caste to protect and promote their interests in education, jobs and politics. In the late 19th and 20th centuries, groups like the South Indian Liberal Federation (Justice Party, 1916), the Ezhava movement (SNDP) and Adi Dravidar organisations demanded representation for non-Brahmins and depressed classes.

items.q: Write about caste discriminatory practices in India.
items.a: Untouchability; denial of temple entry; separate wells, tumblers and burial grounds; denial of education and land; restrictions on dress and use of public roads; forced manual scavenging; endogamy and honour killings; social boycott.

items.q: Explain the recommendations of the Mandal Commission.
items.a: The second Backward Classes Commission under B.P. Mandal (set up 1978-79 under Morarji Desai, report in December 1980) identified 3,743 backward castes making up about 52% of the population and recommended 27% reservation for OBCs in central government jobs and educational institutions, so that total reservation with SC/ST stayed at 50%. V.P. Singh's government implemented it on 13 August 1990; the Supreme Court upheld it in Indra Sawhney (1992), excluding the 'creamy layer'.

items.q: Discuss the basic tenets of an equal society.
items.a:
1. All human beings have equal worth; no one is superior or inferior by birth.
2. Equal rights for all citizens before the law.
3. Equal opportunities in education and employment (a level playing field).
4. No discrimination on caste, religion, race, gender or language.
5. Fair distribution of resources (distributive justice).
6. Basic needs (health, education, nutrition, minimum wages) for all.
7. Special support (reservation, affirmative action) for historically disadvantaged groups.
8. Respect for dignity and diversity; fraternity.

items.q: Give a brief account of the political ideas of Periyar.
items.a:
1. Periyar E.V. Ramasamy founded the Self-Respect Movement (1925) and Dravidar Kazhagam (1944).
2. He fought caste hierarchy and Brahminical domination, saying respecting people by caste is 'barbarian and anti-human'.
3. He demanded communal representation; he left the Congress in 1925 when his resolution at the Kanchipuram conference was rejected.
4. He led the Vaikom Satyagraha against untouchability.
5. He championed women's rights, opposing patriarchy, child marriage and supporting widow remarriage and self-respect marriages.
6. He promoted rationalism against superstition.
7. He agitated for the First Amendment (1951) to protect reservation.

items.q: Discuss the role of various leaders in achieving equality.
items.a:
1. Dr B.R. Ambedkar: fought untouchability, framed constitutional safeguards for SCs and STs.
2. Periyar: Self-Respect Movement, communal representation, women's rights.
3. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule: education of depressed classes and women in Maharashtra.
4. Narayana Guru: organised oppressed castes in Kerala and started schools.
5. Shahu Maharaj of Kolhapur: first introduced reservation (1902).
6. Ayothidasar, Rettamalai Srinivasan, M.C. Rajah: Adi Dravidar rights in Tamil Nadu.
7. Justice Party leaders (Pitti Theagarayar, T.M. Nair, Dr Natesan): Non-Brahmin Manifesto (1916) and communal G.O.s.
8. Mahatma Gandhi: campaign against untouchability.

items.q: Write a note on the leadership of the modern movements for social justice.
items.a:
1. Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation, 1916): Pitti Theagarayar, T.M. Nair and Dr C. Natesan; Non-Brahmin Manifesto; communal G.O.s of 1921-22.
2. Self-Respect Movement (1925) under Periyar: against caste, superstition and gender inequality.
3. Ambedkar's movements: Mahad Satyagraha (1927), Kalaram temple entry, Independent Labour Party, Scheduled Castes Federation.
4. SNDP Yogam (Narayana Guru) in Kerala.
5. Satyashodhak Samaj (Jyotirao Phule) in Maharashtra.
These movements won representation in jobs and education, temple entry, and constitutional safeguards.

items.q: Explain the new social movements.
items.a: New social movements arose from the 1960s-70s around issues of identity, rights and quality of life rather than class alone. Examples: Dalit movements (Dalit Panthers), women's movements, environmental movements (Chipko, Narmada Bachao Andolan), tribal and land-rights movements, human-rights, anti-corruption and LGBTQ movements. They use protests, campaigns, the media and public interest litigation, and work outside party politics to influence policy and widen social justice.
